answer:
HYPOTHESIS (natural-language answer): The highest growth phase of the period between 2000 and 1100 BCE falls in the 15th century BCE (1500–1401 BCE), with the 14th century BCE (1400–1301 BCE) as the sustained runner-up that carries the peak level of activity. During the 15th century BCE every available growth signal peaked simultaneously: the kernel-density estimate of all archaeological finds grew by ~28% over the century (log-difference of kde_all_mean = +0.279; mean KDE growth rate g_all_mean = +0.00283 per year, the highest of all nine centuries), the composite "capital" index (first principal component of the 12 material-culture Z indicators) rose more than in any other century (ΔPC1 = +1.70; mean ΔZ across the 12 indicators = +0.68, with 6 of 12 increasing, led by CopperGold, Depot and HatchetSword), and the land-use/openness proxy rose sharply (mean pollen_grate_100 = +0.0019/yr; Δ pollen_inter_100 = +0.98; Δ SMOOTH_MEAN_100y = +1.00). The 14th century BCE kept strong demographic growth (Δlog kde = +0.14, second-highest; pollen Δ SM100 = +1.36, highest) but shows material-culture stagnation/decline (mean ΔZ = -0.28, 1 of 12 increasing), so the growth *phase* is best described as the 15th–14th centuries BCE, with the 15th century BCE as its unambiguous peak. Growth then reversed: the 13th and especially 12th centuries BCE show the strongest negative demographic trend (g_all_mean = -0.0016 and -0.0044 per year), even though monument-related indicators tick up in the 12th century BCE.

CENTURY CONVENTION: the Nth century BCE is defined as years N000–N001 BCE (the 20th century BCE = 2000–1901 BCE). Shifting all bin boundaries by one year does not change the peak century (15th c. BCE remains top under g_all_mean aggregation).

PER-TRACK RANKINGS (1 = strongest growth):
- Track a, demographic/activity (time_series_data.csv, yearly grain): 15th (g +0.00283/yr, Δlog kde +0.279) > 14th (+0.00145, +0.141) > 16th (+0.00115, +0.109) > 19th > 20th > 17th > 18th > 13th > 12th (most negative).
- Track b, material culture (capital.csv, native 100-y grain): 15th (mean ΔZ +0.68, ΔPC1 +1.70) > 12th (+0.45, +0.76) > 19th (+0.30, +0.68) > 17th > 20th > 16th > 18th > 13th > 14th (-0.28, only 1 of 12 up). The yearly-grain _inter robustness check reproduces these values almost exactly (15th: +0.67).
- Track c, pollen/land use: 15th (grate +0.0019/yr, Δ pollen_inter_100 +0.98, Δ SM100 +1.00) and 14th (Δ SM100 +1.36) clearly lead; 16th c. is the most negative (Δ SM100 -1.74).
- Agreement: the 15th century BCE ranks 1st or 2nd on every track (mean rank 1.14) and is the only century consistently top-ranked; the main conflict is that the 14th century BCE is strong demographically and in pollen but weak in material culture, while the 12th century BCE is strong in material culture but has the most negative demographic trend — these conflicts are reported rather than forced into a single winner.

WORKFLOW: (1) verified time coverage (time_series_data.csv: 3,601 annual rows, CE -4100..-500; pollen file: 4,084 annual rows, calBP 2652..6735; both contain exactly 901 continuous rows for CE -2000..-1100); (2) confirmed capital.csv is the 100-year-grain source of the 12 Z indicators (exact value match, CE = -BCE) and that ts.pollen is identical to the pollen file's Belau_PC1; (3) defined centuries as N000–N001 BCE and computed per-century: mean and cumulative g_all_mean plus endpoint log-difference of kde_all_mean (track a); ΔZ per indicator, mean ΔZ, count of increasing indicators, and Δ of a PCA first-component composite index from capital.csv (track b; _inter columns only as robustness); mean pollen_grate_100, endpoint Δ of pollen_inter_100 and of the pollen file's SMOOTH_MEAN_100y, plus raw-observation counts (track c); (4) ranked centuries per metric and averaged ranks for triangulation; (5) ran a 1-year boundary-shift sensitivity check.

ASSUMPTIONS: CE negative = BCE; g_all_mean and pollen_grate_100 are per-year fractional growth rates with positive = increase (not percentages, not Z-scores); kde_all_mean/kde_all_detrend are densities (points/year), not standardized; the 12 indicator Z-scores are standardized over the full series; the 11th century BCE (1100–1001 BCE) is essentially outside the window (only the year 1100 BCE is present), so peaks are ranked among the 20th–12th centuries BCE.

LIMITATIONS: pollen values are 94.7% interpolated in the window (only 48 raw observations, ~5–6 per century, irregular 10–20 y spacing), so pollen growth estimates carry interpolation-smoothing bias; KDE-based activity/growth partly reflects the sampling density of the underlying finds (taphonomic/research bias) rather than pure demographic change; the _inter columns smooth 100-year observations to yearly grain and were therefore excluded from the headline material-culture result; the century-boundary convention could in principle shift a peak by one century, but the 1-year-shift check leaves the 15th century BCE unchanged; track disagreements (14th c. material culture, 12th c. demographic decline) mean the "growth phase" is 15th–14th c. BCE rather than a single unchallenged century.

payload.hypothesis: The highest growth phase of 2000-1100 BCE occurred in the 15th century BCE (1500-1401 BCE), extending into the 14th century BCE: all three growth tracks (archaeological find density, material-culture capital index, and pollen-based land-use openness) peak in the 15th century BCE, with the 14th century BCE sustaining demographic and land-use growth but not material-culture growth; decline follows in the 13th-12th centuries BCE.

Track b: century-over-century DeltaZ for 12 indicators, mean DeltaZ, count increasing, and DeltaPC1 of a PCA composite from capital.csv at native grain (_inter columns only as robustness). Track c: per-century mean pollen_grate_100, Delta pollen_inter_100, Delta SMOOTH_MEAN_100y, and raw-observation counts.
